rationale: Confirming stored records against original checksums verifies data has not been altered.
Signing builds so any binary modification invalidates the signature protects integrity and attests the build's origin as the development team.
Monitoring for malware and intrusions and isolating the affected component is detecting and containing attacks.
Requires verifying a separately configured secret credential before a change, which is authentication of the account holder.
Establishing the identity of controllers and radar feeds before access is authentication of users and devices.
Requires a valid digital certificate checked against a trusted authority, which is certificate-based authentication.
A keyed HMAC verified on open ensures file content is unchanged; origin or identity verification is not stated.
Single sign-on style session reuse relies on a customer's once-proven identity, so it concerns authentication though it mainly relaxes re-login.
Proving archived tables are identical to the loaded versions is verifying data was not altered.
Refusing connections from clients not on an approved list requires identifying the client as an approved build agent, but what is protected is not stated.
Verifying each clinician's identity via a directory service and denying access without confirmation is authentication.
Requires a credential and verification of the requester's identity against the directory before creating an account.
Verifying the server certificate validity and trust chain before upload authenticates the server.
Requires stored reservation data to remain identical to what was submitted, which is data integrity.
Ensures a superseded credential is rejected at login everywhere, which concerns correct credential-based authentication.
A keyed MAC on each log entry so modification can be detected is an integrity control.
Detecting and blocking SQL injection attempts and notifying the administrator is resisting attack.
Encrypting records at rest protects confidentiality and blocking bulk-extraction through abnormal queries resists abuse.
Rejecting out-of-range commands so stored configuration is not altered protects data integrity, but no attacker is explicitly mentioned.
Access is granted only after a secret passphrase matches the registered one, which is credential authentication.
Validating stored pages against checksums and reporting mismatches detects data corruption or alteration.
Accepting refunds only when they match the original terminal and amount is a consistency validation of transaction data.
Throttling and refusing repeated failed logins to hinder automated guessing contains brute-force attacks.
Single institutional login reused across several services concerns researcher authentication, though it is mostly a convenience requirement.
A server-issued time-limited one-time code for sign-in is a credential for authentication; whether it targets replay attacks is not stated.
Verifying salary and deduction records against checksums and rejecting the run on mismatch protects data integrity.
Entry is allowed after the manager's identity is proven through sign-in, which is authentication.
Verifying each connecting client's identity with a valid credential is authentication.
A digital signature invalidated by any alteration of the agreement protects integrity; origin verification and non-denial are not stated.
Recognising a replayed pairing message and flagging it as an attack is replay-attack detection.
Restricting who may change access rights on tables limits unauthorized modification, an integrity concern.
An encrypted replication protocol so rows cannot be read in transit protects confidentiality.
Signing messages and recomputing log checksums so altered entries are detected protects integrity; origin verification is not stated.
Guaranteeing constants appear unchanged in the binary is a data and program integrity requirement.
Suspending unlock after repeated failures with a waiting period contains brute-force attempts.
Rejecting a concurrent sign-in with a warning may limit account abuse, but the text does not state an attack or identity verification.
Detecting firmware interference and switching devices to fallback settings is a safe state in response to tampering.
Checking that the server certificate is valid, trusted and unaltered authenticates the server and also touches certificate integrity.
Encrypting scenario configuration files during provisioning protects them from disclosure.
